slides.title: Chapter 1: Introduction
slides.say: This deck introduces Bitcoin through true stories, the chapter's key concepts with everyday comparisons, and fifteen short programs. Every number on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library.
slides.takeaway: What Bitcoin is, what it is made of, and why every part of it exists

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: The route has six parts that follow the order of the chapter. Nine true stories and fifteen code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing here can be run and edited there.
slides.takeaway: Six parts, fifteen examples, nine true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.say: These six questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all six has understood the chapter.
slides.takeaway: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

slides.title: One chapter, six branches
slides.say: Chapter 1 says that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem. The six branches are money, network, wallet, usage, foundations and nature. This deck regroups them into six parts.
slides.takeaway: Six branches; every slide today lives on this map

slides.title: Origins
slides.say: Bitcoin did not appear from nothing. This part reads the first block, follows the first payment and meets the cryptographers whose parts Nakamoto combined.
slides.takeaway: Bitcoin combines old parts, like a recipe of familiar ingredients.

slides.title: Origins: key concepts
slides.say: These cards cover Introduction and History of Bitcoin. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A newspaper headline carved into block zero
slides.say: A true story, dated 3 January 2009. Satoshi Nakamoto, the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin, mined block 0 and wrote the headline of that morning's Times into it. The block is a timestamp and a manifesto.
slides.takeaway: Recorded: 3 January 2009

slides.title: The headline inside block zero
slides.say: The first block keeps a short script. Eight bytes of pushes come first, then 69 bytes of text. Decode them and you read The Times of 3 January 2009 inside the chain itself. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: The first block carries its own date: a newspaper headline

slides.title: The first person ever paid in bitcoin
slides.say: A true story, dated 12 January 2009. Hal Finney, who had worked on PGP, was the first person besides Satoshi to run Bitcoin and the first to be paid. One peer paid another, directly.
slides.takeaway: Satoshi Nakamoto, and the cryptographer who ran the code

slides.title: Forty years of failed digital money
slides.say: A true story, dated 31 October 2008. Chaum's company DigiCash went bankrupt; Back's Hashcash priced email with work; b-money and bit gold were never built. Nakamoto added the missing piece and combined them.
slides.takeaway: Every part existed before Bitcoin combined them

slides.title: Four near misses, one combination
slides.say: Chaum's ecash of 1982, Back's Hashcash of 1997, and the b-money and bit gold of 1998 each solved a piece. Nakamoto's paper of 2008 combined them with proof of work as the vote. The genesis block ran in 2009.
slides.takeaway: The pieces were old; the combination was new

slides.title: Money and price
slides.say: Money is a ledger. We see old forms of money, count in satoshis, run the supply schedule and watch a price being discovered by trades, never declared.
slides.takeaway: Money is a ledger of who owns what; Bitcoin keeps that ledger in public.

slides.title: Money and price: key concepts
slides.say: These cards cover floating exchange rate, Finding the Current Price of Bitcoin, currency exchange and Bitcoin ATM. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: The island where money never moved
slides.say: A true story, documented in 1903. On the island of Yap the stones stayed where they lay and the community remembered who owned them. Money is a ledger, and Bitcoin makes the shared memory digital.

read.label: Furness: The Island of Stone Money (book)

slides.takeaway: Documented in 1903; the free ebook edition came in 2024

slides.title: Five thousand years to digital cash
slides.say: A true story, dated 15 August 1971. Money kept changing form, from Mesopotamian grain entries to Lydian coins to bank balances. Cryptocurrency is the next step: a ledger that no single institution keeps.
slides.takeaway: From grain ledgers to pure fiat money, 3000 BCE to 1971

slides.title: Traditional, digital, crypto: side by side
slides.say: Read down a column to see one kind of money, and across a row to see which property changes. Who keeps the ledger is the row that matters most in this course.
slides.takeaway: Same uses, different ledgers: that difference is this course

slides.title: The internet got payments - and new gatekeepers
slides.say: A true story, dated 8 July 2002. The web could sell before it could pay. PayPal solved it by adding a middleman, and the pure digital currencies of the boom failed.
slides.takeaway: The dot-com boom digitised paying, not cash

slides.title: When the money in your hand stops working
slides.say: A true story, dated 26 February 2022. Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's minister of digital transformation, published donation addresses. The next slide lists four more documented cases from 2007 to 2018.
slides.takeaway: Ukraine, February 2022: a state turns to an open payment network

slides.title: When the money in your hand stops working
slides.say: Kenya 2007, Cyprus 2013, Greece 2015, Venezuela 2018 and Ukraine 2022. In each case banks, cards or cash stopped serving people. Each line links to its source.
slides.takeaway: Crisis or war, banked or not: the need is documented

links.label: Source: en.wikipedia.org

links.label: Source: en.wikipedia.org

links.label: Source: en.wikipedia.org

slides.title: A bitcoin counted in satoshis
slides.say: A bitcoin divides into 100 million satoshis. We multiply 0.001 by that number and get exactly 100,000. Amounts in the protocol are whole satoshis, never fractions. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Money here is counting, and the units are exact

slides.title: The subsidy at five block heights
slides.say: The block subsidy starts at fifty bitcoin. The code shifts it right once per era. Five heights give the staircase from 2009 to 2024, each step exactly half of the one before. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Every halving cuts new issuance in half

slides.title: The 21 million cap is a sum
slides.say: Each era issues its subsidy over 210,000 blocks. Adding 33 eras gives 20,999,999.9769 bitcoin. The chart shows the running total approaching 21 million without reaching it. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Scarcity is arithmetic that every node can re-run

slides.title: No one sets the price: trades do
slides.say: Each trade has its own price, found by dividing dollars by bitcoin. A volume-weighted average gives one fair figure for the day. The three trades are illustrative, not market data. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Everyone who trades sets the price a little

slides.title: Two pizzas for ten thousand bitcoin
slides.say: A true story, dated 22 May 2010. Laszlo Hanyecz offered 10,000 bitcoin for two pizzas on a forum and Jeremy Sturdivant ordered them. Price is discovered the first time someone actually pays.
slides.takeaway: 22 May 2010: the day a price began to exist

slides.title: The Pizza Day coins, repriced
slides.say: The pizzas cost 41 dollars of bitcoin in May 2010. The same coins at five later milestones draw the chart; the last point is the price fetched on 6 October 2026. Each gridline is ten times more. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: From 41 dollars to 854 million: price discovery never stopped

slides.title: The network
slides.say: No bank stands in the middle. Every node checks the same rules, proof of work makes history costly to forge, and fees and confirmations settle payments.
slides.takeaway: No bank sits in the middle: shared rules and shared work do its job.

slides.title: A bank in the middle against peers
slides.say: On the left one ledger-keeper sees everything and everyone depends on it. On the right every node checks every rule. Remove one node and the network goes on.
slides.takeaway: Remove any one node and the network still agrees

slides.title: The network: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.say: These cards cover proof of work, consensus and double-spend. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Hard to find, easy to check
slides.say: The search tries numbers until the hash starts with zeros. Each extra zero makes it about sixteen times longer on average. Anyone checks the winner with a single hash. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Finding takes thousands of guesses; checking takes one hash

slides.title: Mining pays for honesty
slides.say: Transactions wait, miners spend energy on proof of work, a block is found about every ten minutes, and the finder earns subsidy plus fees. Cheating costs more than it could win.
slides.takeaway: Security is bought with energy and paid in bitcoin

slides.title: Why digital money had to wait
slides.say: A digital coin is only a file, and files copy perfectly. Both copies could be spent. For decades only a trusted central ledger could stop that, so digital money meant bank money.
slides.takeaway: A file can be copied; a coin must not be

slides.title: The double-spend, solved in public
slides.say: Every payment is broadcast and the nodes agree on one order. The first spend of a coin enters the block, and every node refuses the second. The next code slide runs that rule.
slides.takeaway: Agreement on order is what removes the referee

slides.title: A double spend is refused
slides.say: A ledger remembers which coins are spent. Alice pays Bob with coin c1 and it is accepted. When she offers the same coin to Carol, the rule refuses it, and no bank decides. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: The second spend of a coin is refused everywhere

slides.title: A chain that notices tampering
slides.say: Each block's hash covers its own text and the hash of the block before. Changing one word in block two makes the check stop there, so nothing after it can be trusted. It is example 9 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Change one old block and every later link fails

slides.title: The network: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.say: These cards cover confirmation and transaction fee. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: What the outputs leave over is the fee
slides.say: A coin of 100,000 satoshis pays 20,000 to Bob and returns 75,000 as change. The 5,000 left over goes to the miner who includes the payment. Fees are implied, never written. It is example 10 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: The fee is the part of the coin nobody was given

slides.title: Wallets and keys
slides.say: A wallet holds keys, not coins. This part sorts wallets by platform, by how much of the network they check, and by who holds the keys and the backup.
slides.takeaway: A wallet holds keys, not coins, like a ring of keys to many safes.

slides.title: The wallet branch, mapped
slides.say: A wallet is classified by its platform, by how much of the network it checks, by who holds the keys, and by how it is backed up. Every leaf has a card in this part.
slides.takeaway: Four questions place any wallet on this map

slides.title: Wallets and keys: key concepts (1 of 4)
slides.say: These cards cover Getting Started, Choosing a Bitcoin Wallet, Types of Bitcoin wallets and desktop wallet. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Wallets and keys: key concepts (2 of 4)
slides.say: These cards cover mobile wallet, web wallet, hardware signing device and third-party API client. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Wallets and keys: key concepts (3 of 4)
slides.say: These cards cover full node, lightweight client, Full node versus Lightweight and Who controls the keys. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Your key is your deed
slides.say: Access to bitcoin is controlled by private keys, like very long PINs. With a house, the key opens the door and a registry proves the owner. In Bitcoin the key is both, so it must prove without being shown.
slides.takeaway: Prove you hold the key; never reveal it

slides.title: Whoever holds the keys holds the coins
slides.say: With full control you keep the keys, sign yourself and carry the backup. With third-party control a service keeps the keys, which is convenient, and you trust its honesty and uptime. Every wallet type can be either.
slides.takeaway: Custody is the first security decision you make

slides.title: The exchange that lost everyone's coins
slides.say: A true story, dated 28 February 2014. Mt. Gox was once the largest bitcoin exchange. Whoever holds the keys holds the coins, exchanges included. This is the cost of a custodial wallet.
slides.takeaway: Tokyo, February 2014: balances on a website, keys elsewhere

slides.title: Wallets and keys: key concepts (4 of 4)
slides.say: These cards cover noncustodial wallet and Recovery Codes. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A recovery phrase becomes a seed
slides.say: A recovery phrase of twelve words is stretched by repeating a keyed hash. With 1, 10 or 2048 rounds the seeds look unrelated. A thief guessing phrases pays all 2048 rounds per guess. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Slow on purpose: every guess costs the full 2048 rounds

slides.title: A first payment
slides.say: We follow a first payment from an empty wallet. First how to get bitcoin, then what an address and an invoice are, and finally how a wallet sends with change.
slides.takeaway: From an empty wallet to a first payment, like a first driving lesson.

slides.title: A first payment: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.say: These cards cover Quick Start, Bitcoin Addresses, Bitcoin address and invoice. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Alice's first bitcoin, step by step
slides.say: Alice installs a wallet, which makes her keys and a recovery code. She shares an address, acquires her first bitcoin, and waits for confirmations. The next slides build each step.
slides.takeaway: Four steps from an empty phone to a first payment

slides.title: An address is a hash with a checksum
slides.say: Block 0 pays to a 20-byte key hash behind a version byte. The checksum is the first four bytes of a double hash. Together they make 25 bytes, written in Base58 as a 34-character address. It is example 12 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: A mistyped address is caught by its checksum

slides.title: An invoice is a link with an amount
slides.say: A payment request packs an address, an amount, a label and a message into one text. The wallet splits it into named fields and turns the amount into whole satoshis. It is example 13 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: A QR code is only this text, drawn as dots

slides.title: A first payment: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.say: These cards cover Receiving Bitcoin, Getting Your First Bitcoin and Sending and Receiving Bitcoin. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Sending: coins in, payment and change out
slides.say: The wallet owes 60,000 satoshis plus a 1,500 fee. It picks the smallest coin that covers both, 80,000, and sends 18,500 back to itself as change. It is example 14 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: You never cut a coin: you spend it and get change

slides.title: Foundations
slides.say: Two old ideas, proof of work and agreement without trust, meet in Bitcoin. Payment channels keep many payments off the chain, and four adjectives name its nature.
slides.takeaway: Two old solved problems, joined into one system, like two rivers.

slides.title: Two solved problems, one new system
slides.say: Hashcash of 1997 makes sending cost computation. The Byzantine Generals' problem of 1982 asks how parties that cannot trust each other agree. Proof of work with the longest valid chain is Bitcoin's practical answer.
slides.takeaway: Neither idea was new; their combination was

slides.title: From keys to the chain
slides.say: Keys make addresses, addresses receive transactions, transactions are gathered into blocks, and blocks are added by mining. Each stage trusts only what it can verify. Later chapters open each box.
slides.takeaway: This pipeline is the course syllabus in one row

slides.title: Foundations: key concepts
slides.say: These cards cover offchain technology. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Two transactions, any number of payments
slides.say: On the chain every payment is a transaction. A channel needs one to open and one to close, whatever happens between. One payment alone costs more; a thousand save 998 transactions. It is example 15 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: A channel pays off from the third payment on

slides.title: What kind of thing is Bitcoin?
slides.say: The chapter gives two answers. Bitcoin is virtual, borderless, decentralized and robust, and it is built from a peer-to-peer protocol, a public journal and a consensus rule set. Each adjective is engineered.
slides.takeaway: Each adjective is engineered, not advertised

slides.title: The chapter in six lines
slides.say: Six lines, one per part. If any line still feels like a claim rather than a fact, go back to the slide that carries its receipt. The course page for chapter 1 has the full text and the question bank.
slides.takeaway: If a line feels unproven, its code slide carries the receipt

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.say: Everything here is free to read or watch. A good start is the white paper, nine pages, and then the 3Blue1Brown video. The block explorers let you look up the first block and the pizza payment yourself.
